title: Building REST APIs with FastAPI
summary: Expose your Python logic to the world by building fast, typed, auto-documented web APIs with the FastAPI framework.
objectives: Explain what a REST API is and how HTTP methods map to actions
Create a FastAPI app and run it with the Uvicorn server
Define GET and POST endpoints with path and query parameters
Validate request bodies using Pydantic models
Return correct status codes and JSON responses
Use the auto-generated interactive docs to test your API

quiz.q: In REST, which HTTP method is conventionally used to create a new resource?
quiz.why: POST sends data to the server to create a new resource. GET retrieves, PUT/PATCH update, and DELETE removes.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a Pydantic model in FastAPI?
options: Validate and parse incoming request data
quiz.why: Pydantic models declare the expected shape and types; FastAPI uses them to validate, parse, and document the request body automatically.

quiz.q: Which HTTP status code means 'created successfully'?
quiz.why: 201 Created signals a new resource was made. 200 is generic OK, 404 is not found, and 500 is a server error.

quiz.q: What command runs a FastAPI app where the FastAPI instance is named 'app' in a file called main.py?
quiz.why: Uvicorn is the ASGI server. 'main:app' points to the app object in main.py, and --reload restarts on code changes during development.

quiz.q: By default, at which URL path can you find FastAPI's interactive Swagger documentation?
quiz.why: FastAPI auto-generates interactive Swagger UI at /docs and an alternative ReDoc page at /redoc from your code and type hints.

quiz.q: True or false — FastAPI uses standard Python type hints to validate and convert request data.
quiz.why: True. FastAPI reads your type hints to validate input, convert types, and build documentation, which is a big reason it is so concise.

body_markdown:
## What is a REST API?

An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a way for programs to talk to each other. A **REST API** does this over HTTP — the same protocol your browser uses. A client sends a **request** to a URL using a **method** (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), and the server sends back a **response**, usually as JSON.

The methods map to actions: **GET** reads data, **POST** creates, **PUT/PATCH** update, and **DELETE** removes. This lets the maths logic you have been writing become a service other apps — and AI products — can call.

## FastAPI and your first endpoint

**FastAPI** is a modern Python framework for building APIs. It is fast, uses ordinary type hints, and generates interactive docs for free. Install it together with the **Uvicorn** server.

```bash
pip install "fastapi[standard]" uvicorn
```

A route is just a function with a decorator that says which method and path it answers.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/")
def read_root():
    return {"message": "Hello, API!"}
```

## Running the server

Uvicorn serves your app. The `--reload` flag restarts it whenever you save a file.

```bash
uvicorn main:app --reload
```

Now visit `http://127.0.0.1:8000` for the response and `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` for the interactive Swagger documentation, where you can try every endpoint in the browser.

## Path and query parameters

Values inside the URL path become **path parameters**; type hints convert and validate them. Extra options after a `?` are **query parameters**.

```python
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
def get_item(item_id: int, q: str | None = None):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "q": q}
```

Here FastAPI guarantees `item_id` is an integer — send text and it returns a clear 422 error automatically.

## Request bodies with Pydantic

To accept structured data, declare a **Pydantic model**. FastAPI validates the incoming JSON against it, parses it, and documents it for you.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float
    in_stock: bool = True

@app.post("/items", status_code=201)
def create_item(item: Item):
    return {"created": item.name, "price": item.price}
```

Notice `status_code=201` — we return the correct "created" code rather than a plain 200.

## Your task

Build a small **books API**: a Pydantic `Book` model, a GET endpoint to list books, and a POST endpoint to add one. Test it all from the `/docs` page.

slides.title: Building REST APIs with FastAPI
slides.sub: Month 2 - Data, SQL & Web APIs  |  Lesson 9
slides.narration: Welcome back. So far you've written Python logic and pulled data from databases. In this lesson we make that logic available to the outside world by building a web A P I. We'll use FastAPI, a modern Python framework, to create endpoints, validate input, and get interactive documentation for free. This is exactly how real A I products expose their models.

slides.title: What is a REST API?
bullets: An A P I lets programs talk to each other.
REST works over HTTP, returning JSON.
Client sends a request, server sends a response.
slides.narration: Let's start with the idea. An A P I is simply a way for one program to talk to another. A REST A P I does this over HTTP, the same protocol your browser uses. A client sends a request to a U R L, and the server replies with a response, usually formatted as Jason. This is how your maths code can become a service other apps call.

slides.title: HTTP methods map to actions
bullets: GET reads data.
POST creates new data.
PUT and PATCH update; DELETE removes.
slides.narration: REST uses HTTP methods to describe what you want to do. GET reads or fetches data. POST creates something new. PUT and PATCH update existing data, and DELETE removes it. Keeping these meanings consistent is what makes an A P I predictable and easy for other developers to use.

slides.title: Your first FastAPI app
bullets: Create a FastAPI instance called app.
Decorate a function with the method and path.
Return a dict; FastAPI turns it into JSON.
slides.narration: Here is a complete A P I. We import FastAPI and create an app object. Then we write an ordinary function and decorate it with at-app-dot-get and a path. That decorator says: when someone sends a GET request to this path, run this function. We return a Python dictionary, and FastAPI automatically converts it into a Jason response.

slides.title: Running with Uvicorn
bullets: Uvicorn is the server that runs your app.
main:app points to the app in main.py.
--reload restarts on every code change.
slides.narration: FastAPI describes your A P I, but Uvicorn actually serves it. We run uvicorn, then main colon app, which means the app object inside main dot py. The reload flag restarts the server automatically every time you save, which is perfect while you're developing. Your A P I is now live on localhost, port eight thousand.

slides.title: Free interactive docs
bullets: Visit /docs for interactive Swagger UI.
Try every endpoint right in the browser.
Built automatically from your code.
slides.narration: Here's a feature you'll love. Go to slash docs in your browser, and FastAPI gives you a full interactive documentation page. You can see every endpoint and actually call them with real data, all without writing a line of documentation yourself. It's generated automatically from your functions and type hints.

slides.title: Path & query parameters
bullets: Path values like {item_id} go in the U R L.
Type hints validate and convert them.
Options after ? are query parameters.
slides.narration: Often you need to pass values in. Anything inside curly braces in the path becomes a path parameter. Because we hinted item underscore i d as an int, FastAPI checks it really is a number and converts it for you. Anything else, like q here, becomes a query parameter, the part after the question mark in a U R L.

slides.title: Validate with Pydantic
bullets: A Pydantic model declares the data shape.
FastAPI validates incoming JSON against it.
Bad data returns a clear 422 error.
slides.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float
    in_stock: bool = True
slides.narration: For richer data, we use a Pydantic model. We subclass BaseModel and list the fields with their types. When a request comes in, FastAPI checks the incoming Jason matches this shape. If a field is missing or the wrong type, the caller gets a clear four-two-two error explaining exactly what went wrong. You write the model; validation comes free.

slides.title: Accepting a POST body
bullets: Type the parameter as your model.
FastAPI parses the JSON into an object.
Set status_code=201 for created.
slides.narration: Now we accept data with POST. We add a parameter typed as our Item model, and FastAPI reads the request body, validates it, and hands us a ready-made object. Notice we set status code two-oh-one, which is the correct code for something created, rather than a plain two hundred. Returning the right status code is good A P I manners.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Forgetting --reload, so changes don't show.
Missing type hints, so no validation.
Returning 200 when you created something.
Editing the wrong file path in main:app.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One: forgetting the reload flag and wondering why your changes don't appear. Two: leaving off type hints, which switches off the validation you came here for. Three: returning a plain two hundred when you actually created a resource. And four: pointing uvicorn at the wrong module or app name. Watch these and you'll debug far less.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: REST maps HTTP methods to actions over JSON.
Decorators define endpoints; Uvicorn serves them.
Type hints and Pydantic validate your data.
Visit /docs to test everything live.
Task: build a small books A P I.
slides.narration: Let's recap. A REST A P I maps HTTP methods onto actions and speaks Jason. In FastAPI you define endpoints with decorators and serve them with Uvicorn. Type hints and Pydantic models validate your data automatically, and the slash docs page lets you test it all live. Your task: build a small books A P I with a Pydantic model, a GET to list books, and a POST to add one. Brilliant work, and I'll see you in the next lesson.
